Why the regular sprites look mostly empty. They are layers, not icons: all 22 bots and all their parts are rendered through one camera, sized so the widest bot fits, and each part keeps its place on that canvas. That is what lets any head sit on any legs with no offsets. Stacking a bot’s own layers reproduces its full-body sprite with a worst-case alpha error of 0.00%; up to 3.9% of pixels differ in shade, because a part rendered alone receives no shadow from the part next to it. trimRect in the manifest gives each layer’s tight box, for an atlas that wants to pack them.

Every bot is aligned at the neck. The rips were sized by bounding box, so tails pushed bodies forward and horns pulled them back, and necks scattered 0.61 m front to back. Each bot is now moved, whole and unscaled, so the point where its head meets its body lands on Tinpet (Male)’s neck — any head seats on any body. The accepted cost: feet no longer share one floor (they sit up to 23 cm apart), and shoulders keep their own anatomy, so arms land close to another bot’s shoulders but not on them (median miss about 10 cm).

Three parts: head, arms, legs. Legs means everything below the head that is not an arm — torso and legs together, which the rips deliver as one mesh anyway. The head is kept as the source game cut it, which on several bots runs down through the chest armour.

Arms are one part, three sprites. From a 3/4 view one arm is usually behind the body and the other in front of it, so no single layer can sit at one place in a draw order: the stage draws arms_back and arms_front separately. Where the back arm goes is measured, not assumed — shoulder-mounted weapons sit far enough forward that on Arcbeetle, Metabee, Rhinorush even the far arm overlaps the body from in front. Each bot’s slot comes from its own full render, and a mixed build uses the slot of the bot the arms came from.
